category: Mutual Funds and Systematic Investment Plans
title: Mutual Funds Overview, Net Asset Value (NAV) & Total Expense Ratio (TER)
questions: What is a mutual fund?
What is Net Asset Value (NAV)?
What is Total Expense Ratio (TER)?
What is the difference between direct and regular mutual fund plans?
content: Mutual funds pool money from investors to purchase a diversified portfolio of stocks, bonds, or money-market securities managed by an Asset Management Company (AMC) under SEBI regulations: (1) Net Asset Value (NAV): The per-unit market value of a mutual fund scheme, calculated daily at market close. NAV = (Total Market Value of Assets - Liabilities & Expenses) / Total Outstanding Units. (2) Total Expense Ratio (TER): The annual percentage fee charged by the AMC to manage the fund (fund manager fees, administration, marketing), capped by SEBI based on AUM tiers. (3) Direct vs Regular Plans: Direct plans carry zero distributor commission, resulting in a lower TER (0.5% to 1.5% lower) and delivering significantly higher compounded returns over long horizons.
source: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations 1996 & AMFI Investor Education Handbooks

category: Mutual Funds and Systematic Investment Plans
title: Systematic Investment Plan (SIP), Rupee Cost Averaging & SWP Explained
questions: What is a Systematic Investment Plan (SIP)?
How does rupee cost averaging work in SIP?
What is a Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP)?
Is SIP better than lump-sum investment?
content: Structured investment approaches that eliminate the need to time financial markets: (1) Systematic Investment Plan (SIP): An automated facility allowing investors to invest a fixed sum (e.g. ₹500, ₹5,000) at regular intervals (monthly/quarterly) into a mutual fund scheme. (2) Rupee Cost Averaging: In falling markets, your fixed instalment automatically purchases more fund units at lower NAVs; in rising markets, it buys fewer units at higher NAVs, reducing the average cost per unit over time without stress. (3) Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP): The inverse of SIP; allows investors (such as retirees) to redeem a fixed sum monthly from their mutual fund corpus while the remaining capital continues compounding.
source: Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI) Investor Guidelines

category: Mutual Funds and Systematic Investment Plans
title: Equity, Debt, Hybrid & Index Mutual Funds (SEBI Scheme Categorization)
questions: What are the main categories of mutual funds in India?
What is the difference between large cap, mid cap, and small cap funds?
What is an index fund?
How are hybrid mutual funds structured?
content: Under SEBI's Scheme Categorization Circular, mutual funds follow strict asset allocation mandates: (1) Equity Schemes: Invest primarily in equities. Categories include Large-Cap (top 100 companies by market cap, minimum 80% equity), Mid-Cap (101st to 250th companies, min 65%), Small-Cap (251st onwards, min 65%), Flexi-Cap (dynamic allocation across market caps), and ELSS (tax-saving equity with 3-year lock-in). (2) Debt Schemes: Invest in fixed-income securities (G-Secs, corporate bonds, commercial paper) categorized by duration (Liquid, Overnight, Short Duration, Corporate Bond). (3) Hybrid Schemes: Blend equity and debt (e.g. Aggressive Hybrid: 65-80% equity, 20-35% debt). (4) Index Funds: Passively replicate market indices (Nifty 50, Sensex) with low expense ratios.
source: SEBI Master Circular on Categorization and Rationalization of Mutual Fund Schemes

category: Mutual Funds and Systematic Investment Plans
title: Direct Plans vs Regular Plans: Compounding Effect of Lower Total Expense Ratios
questions: What is the difference between direct and regular mutual fund plans?
How much extra returns do direct mutual funds give?
Do direct mutual funds have the same portfolio as regular plans?
Why does the NAV of a direct plan stay higher than a regular plan?
content: Since January 2013, SEBI mandated that every mutual fund scheme must offer two distinct purchase routes: (1) Regular Plan: Purchased through mutual fund distributors, brokers, or banks. The AMC pays an ongoing trail commission (typically 0.50% to 1.50% per year) to the distributor out of the fund's assets, increasing the Total Expense Ratio (TER). (2) Direct Plan: Purchased directly from the AMC or direct investment platforms without an intermediary. Has zero distributor commissions, resulting in a substantially lower TER. (3) Compounding Impact: Over a 20-year horizon, saving 1% annually in TER can result in a 20% to 30% larger final retirement corpus.
source: SEBI Directives on Introduction of Direct Plans in Mutual Funds

category: Mutual Funds and Systematic Investment Plans
title: Equity Linked Savings Schemes (ELSS): 3-Year Lock-In & Section 80C Benefits
questions: What is ELSS in mutual funds?
How long is the lock-in period for ELSS mutual funds?
How does an ELSS SIP lock-in work?
Is ELSS better than PPF and tax-saver FD?
content: Equity Linked Savings Schemes (ELSS) are diversified equity mutual funds notified by the Central Government: (1) Tax Deduction: Investments up to ₹1,50,000 per financial year qualify for tax deduction under Section 80C (Old Tax Regime). (2) Shortest Lock-In: Features a mandatory 3-year lock-in period—the shortest among all Section 80C tax-saving instruments (compared to 5 years for Tax-Saver FDs, 15 years for PPF). (3) SIP Lock-in Mechanics: When investing in ELSS via monthly SIP, each monthly instalment has its own independent 3-year lock-in clock from the date of that specific purchase. (4) Returns: Long-term capital gains above ₹1.25 Lakh are taxed at 12.5%.
source: Equity Linked Savings Scheme 2005 Guidelines & Income Tax Act Section 80C

category: Mutual Funds and Systematic Investment Plans
title: Mutual Fund Capital Gains Tax: 2024 LTCG (12.5%) and STCG (20%) Rules
questions: What is the capital gains tax on equity mutual funds in India?
How much long term capital gains is tax free in equity mutual funds?
How are debt mutual funds taxed after April 2023?
What is the holding period for long term capital gains in mutual funds?
content: Taxation of mutual funds under the revised Finance (No. 2) Act 2024: (1) Equity Mutual Funds (≥65% equity allocation): (a) Short-Term Capital Gains (STCG, held ≤ 12 months): Taxed at 20% (increased from 15%). (b) Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG, held > 12 months): Taxed at 12.5% (increased from 10%) on gains exceeding an annual tax-free threshold of ₹1,25,000 (increased from ₹1 Lakh). (2) Debt Mutual Funds (<35% equity): Specified debt funds acquired on or after April 1, 2023 have zero indexation benefits; all gains are treated as short-term and taxed at the investor's applicable marginal income-tax slab rates.
source: Finance (No. 2) Act 2024 & CBDT Notifications on Capital Gains Taxation

category: Mutual Funds and Systematic Investment Plans
title: Systematic Transfer Plan (STP) & Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP) Mechanics
questions: What is a Systematic Transfer Plan (STP) in mutual funds?
How does STP prevent investing a lump-sum at market peaks?
How does SWP work as a monthly pension for retirees?
Does an STP transfer trigger capital gains tax?
content: Automated asset allocation mechanisms across mutual fund schemes: (1) Systematic Transfer Plan (STP): Allows an investor holding a lump-sum corpus to park the money in a low-risk Liquid or Ultra-Short Duration debt fund, while automatically transferring a fixed sum weekly or monthly into an equity fund. Staggers market entry to mitigate market-peak risk. (2) Tax Implication: Each STP transfer is legally treated as a redemption from the source fund, triggering capital gains calculation. (3) Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP): Generates tax-efficient regular monthly cash flows for retirees by redeeming units, where tax applies only on the gain component of each redeemed unit.
source: AMFI Best Practice Guidelines on Systematic Investment & Transfer Facilities

category: Mutual Funds and Systematic Investment Plans
title: Exit Load Charges, Holding Horizons and Mutual Fund Stamp Duty (0.005%)
questions: What is an exit load in mutual funds?
How much exit load is charged if I redeem equity funds before 1 year?
Why was a 0.005% stamp duty introduced on mutual fund purchases?
Do liquid funds have an exit load?
content: Transaction levies and holding penalties governing mutual fund redemptions: (1) Exit Load: A fractional percentage deduction (typically 1.0%) levied by AMCs if units are redeemed before completing a pre-defined minimum holding period (e.g. 1 year for equity funds, 30-90 days for hybrid funds). The exit load is credited back into the scheme's assets to protect remaining long-term unit holders. (2) Liquid Funds Graded Exit Load: Under SEBI norms, liquid funds impose a graded exit load on redemptions made within 7 days of investment (0.0070% on Day 1 scaling to 0% by Day 8). (3) Stamp Duty: A mandatory federal stamp duty of 0.005% is deducted upfront on all purchases and SIPs.
source: SEBI Circular on Graded Exit Load in Liquid Funds & Indian Stamp Act Amendments

category: Mutual Funds and Systematic Investment Plans
title: AMFI Code of Conduct for Mutual Fund Distributors & Risk Profiling
questions: What is an ARN number in mutual funds?
Can a mutual fund distributor guarantee returns?
What is portfolio churning by brokers?
What are the ethical rules for mutual fund agents in India?
content: Regulatory ethics governing AMFI-registered mutual fund distributors (MFDs / ARN holders): (1) Mandatory Licensing: Distributors must pass NISM certification and hold a valid AMFI Registration Number (ARN). (2) Prohibition of Guarantees: Under SEBI regulations, distributors are strictly prohibited from promising, advertising, or guaranteeing fixed or assured returns on any mutual fund product. (3) Ban on Churning: Inducing clients to redeem existing profitable funds merely to invest in new fund offerings (NFOs) to generate fresh commissions ('churning') is a severe code violation. (4) Suitability Mandate: Must conduct mandatory investor risk profiling.
source: AMFI Code of Ethics and Guidelines for Intermediaries & SEBI Regulations

category: Mutual Funds and Systematic Investment Plans
title: Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) vs Active Mutual Funds: Tracking Errors & Liquidity
questions: What is the difference between an ETF and an index mutual fund?
Do I need a Demat account to buy ETFs in India?
What is tracking error in exchange traded funds?
Why do ETFs have lower expense ratios than active funds?
content: Comparing passive index replication methods with actively managed portfolios: (1) Operational Structure: Active funds employ fund managers attempting to outperform benchmark indices through stock picking; ETFs passively track an underlying index (e.g. Nifty 50, Gold, Bank Nifty). (2) Trading Mechanics: Unlike mutual funds where transactions execute at end-of-day NAV, ETFs trade continuously on stock exchanges (NSE/BSE) during market hours at real-time market prices; requires a Demat and trading account. (3) Tracking Error & Difference: The standard deviation of the difference in returns between the ETF and its underlying benchmark. ETFs carry the lowest TERs in the market (0.05% to 0.20%).
source: SEBI Circular on Development of Passive Funds Framework & ETFs

category: Mutual Funds and Systematic Investment Plans
title: Liquid Funds, Overnight Funds & Arbitrage Funds for Ultra-Short Surpluses
questions: Where should I park surplus money for 1 to 3 months?
What is an arbitrage fund and how is it taxed as equity?
How safe are overnight mutual funds?
How fast can I withdraw money from a liquid fund?
content: Optimizing short-term cash management with high liquidity and low volatility: (1) Overnight Funds: Invest in securities with a maturity of 1 single day (CBLO/TREPS), carrying practically zero interest rate and credit default risk. (2) Liquid Funds: Invest in commercial paper and treasury bills with residual maturities up to 91 days. Offer instant redemption facilities (up to ₹50,000 or 90% of folio value credited within minutes 24x7). (3) Arbitrage Funds: Exploit price differentials between the cash (spot) market and futures market. Because they maintain ≥65% gross equity exposure, they enjoy equity taxation (12.5% LTCG, 20% STCG) while behaving with debt-like stability.
source: SEBI Scheme Categorization Circular & Product Descriptions

category: Mutual Funds and Systematic Investment Plans
title: SEBI Scheme Categorization: Strict Asset Allocation Ratios & Overlap Limits
questions: Why did SEBI standardize mutual fund categories?
Can a mutual fund company have two large-cap equity funds?
How does SEBI define large-cap, mid-cap, and small-cap stocks?
What is portfolio overlap in mutual funds?
content: In 2017, SEBI enacted historic reforms to eradicate misleading fund nomenclature and reduce consumer confusion: (1) One Scheme Per Category Rule: An AMC can launch only one scheme per defined category (with exceptions for Index Funds/ETFs, Sectoral/Thematic funds, and Fund of Funds), stopping the practice of launching duplicate schemes. (2) Statutory Market Cap Lists: AMFI publishes official lists semi-annually categorizing all listed companies: Large Cap (1st to 100th), Mid Cap (101st to 250th), and Small Cap (251st onwards). Mutual funds must rebalance portfolios within statutory timelines to maintain compliant ratios.
source: SEBI Master Circular on Categorization and Rationalization of Mutual Fund Schemes
